query: How can we decompose the overall DiD into cohort comparisons (Goodman-Bacon) and report decomposition weights?

response.query: How can we decompose the overall DiD into cohort comparisons (Goodman-Bacon) and report decomposition weights?
response.answer: The overall DiD estimate can be decomposed into cohort comparisons using the Goodman-Bacon method, which assigns weights based on relative data coverage. The weighted sum of these estimates equals the original DiD coefficient. The decomposition highlights the relative influence of different treatment timings.

results.title: bacon-decomp | DiD
results.content: As discussed at the end of the TWFE section, the introduction of differential treatment timing makes it hard to draw a bright line between *pre* and *post* treatment periods. ggplot(dat4, aes(x = tt, y = y, col = factor(id))) + geom_point() + geom_line() + geom_vline(xintercept = c(4.5, 7.5), lty = 2) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales:: pretty_breaks()) + labs(x = "Time variable", y = "Outcome variable", col = "ID"). The first treatment occurs to period 5, where id=2’s trendline jumps by 2 units. The second treatment occurs in period 8, where id=3’s trendline jumps by 4 units. For example, how should the late treated unit (id=3) regard the early treated unit (id=2)? In other words, the panel IDs are split into different timing cohorts based on when the first treatment takes place and where it lies in relation to the treatment of other panel IDs. The more panel IDs and differential treatment timings there are, the more the combinations of the above groups. The Goodman-Bacon decomposition isolates each of these 2x2 comparisons and assigns them a weight, based on their relative coverage in the data (i.e., how long each comparison lasts relative to the overall timespan, and how many units were involved). treated untreated estimate weight type 2 5 Inf 2 0.3636364 Treated vs Untreated 3 8 Inf 4 0.3181818 Treated vs Untreated 6 8 5 4 0.1363636 Later vs Earlier Treated 8 5 8 2 0.1818182 Earlier vs Later Treated. The table tells us that (\(T\) vs \(U\)), which is the sum of the late and early treated versus never treated, has the largest weight, followed by early vs late treated, and lastly, late vs early treated. Importantly, note that the weighted mean of these estimates is exactly the same as our earlier (naive) TWFE coefficient estimate. ggplot(bgd, aes(x = weight, y = estimate, shape = type, col = type)) + geom_hline(yintercept = bgd_wm, lty = 2) + geom_point(size = 3) + labs( x = "Weight", y = "Estimate", shape = "Type", col = "Type", title = "Bacon-Goodman decomposition example", caption = "Note: The horizontal dotted line depicts the full TWFE estimate." ). * *Treated vs Untreated* (two blue squares; one for the earlier treated group and another for the later treated group).

results.title: bacon
results.content: `bacon()` is a function that decomposes two-way fixed effects models into all 2x2 estimates and their weights following Goodman-Bacon (2019). The authors estimate the effect of “castle doctrines,” state laws that make it easier to use lethal force in self defense. The data set `castle` contains state/year level information from 2000-2010 on crime rates and whether or not the state had a castle doctrine in effect. First, we perform the decomposition without time-varying controls, and make sure that the weighted average of the decomposition equals the two-way fixed effects estimate. library bacon ~ data =::id_var = "state"time_var = "year"#> type weight avg_est#> 1 Earlier vs Later Treated 0.05976 -0.00554#> 2 Later vs Earlier Treated 0.03190 0.07032#> 3 Treated vs Untreated 0.90834 0.08796 sum $* $ print paste"Weighted sum of decomposition =" round 4#> [1] "Weighted sum of decomposition = 0.0818" lm ~ + factor + factordata =:: print paste"Two-way FE estimate =" round $ 2 4#> [1] "Two-way FE estimate = 0.0818". Now, we plot each 2x2 estimate and its weight to see what is driving the result. library ggplot + aesx =y =shape = factor + labsx = "Weight"y = "Estimate"shape = "Type" + geom_point. In this example, one estimate has almost 60 percent of the weight: states treated in 2006 vs states that are never treated. \(\Omega\) is the weight given to this estimate in the two-way fixed effects estimate. For each treatment group dyad, there is only one estimate, \(\hat{\beta}^d\_{b, k, l}\) which gets weight \(s\_{k, l}\). The two way fixed effects estimate, \(\hat{\beta}^{DD|X}\), then decomposes to:. bacon ~ + + data =::id_var = "state"time_var = "year"#> type weight avg_est#> 1 Both Treated 0.09121 0.02724#> 2 Treated vs Untreated 0.90879 0.09002 $ weighted.mean $ $ $ $ $ * + 1 - * print paste"Weighted sum of decomposition =" round 4#> [1] "Weighted sum of decomposition = 0.0906" lm ~ + + + factor + factordata =:: $ "post" print paste"Two way FE estimate =" round 4#> [1] "Two way FE estimate = 0.0906". And again we can plot the decomposed between estimates, \(\hat{\beta}^d\_{b, k, l}\) and their weights, \(s\_{k, l}\). ggplot $ + aesx =y =shape = factor + labsx = "Weight"y = "Estimate" + geom_point.

results.title: R: Goodman-Bacon Decomposition
results.content: ## Goodman-Bacon Decomposition. ### Description. bacon() is a function that performs the Goodman-Bacon decomposition for differences-in-differences with variation in treatment timing (with or without time-varying covariates). ### Usage. bacon(formula, data, id_var, time_var, quietly = F). ### Arguments. ### Value. If control variables are included in the formula, then an object of class "list" with three elements:. If not control variables are included then only the two\_by\_twos data.frame is returned. ### Examples. # Castle Doctrine (Uncontrolled) df_bacon <- bacon(l_homicide ~ post, data = bacondecomp::castle, id_var = "state", time_var = "year") # Castle Doctrine (Controlled) ret_bacon <- bacon(l_homicide ~ post + l_pop + l_income, data = bacondecomp::castle, id_var = "state", time_var = "year"). Package *bacondecomp* version 0.1.1 [Index].
